clue.text: Two novelists contribute to Bridges work

parts.note: Jack London, the American author of The Call of the Wild
C. P. Snow, the English author of the Strangers and Brothers sequence

explanation.surface: A pair of novelists lend a hand with a building project on bridges.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Bridges, Poet Laureate, wrote the poem named here; 'Bridges' looks like engineering, but it is the poet.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem of that title, about a city under a white fall, is by the Poet Laureate Robert Bridges.

clue.text: A single book in French might mean a lifetime's work for us

definitions.meaning: in French the word names one written work, such as a single book
in English the borrowed word means the whole body of an artist's or writer's output

explanation.surface: One French book might add up to a whole career's output for an English reader.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for a single piece of work is borrowed into English for a writer's complete output.

clue.text: Possibly rid Sulla of another dictator's sister

indicators.note: possibly says the letters could be arranged some other way, so rework them

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written: the Roman dictator's name

explanation.surface: Perhaps one could free the Roman dictator Sulla from a rival tyrant's sibling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' reworks RID SULLA. The other dictator is Caligula, whose sister was Drusilla.
explanation.definitionFit: Drusilla was the sister of the Roman emperor Caligula, a tyrant like Sulla.

clue.text: Hardly a novel category for librarians

definitions.text: Hardly a novel category for librarians

parts.words: Hardly a novel category for librarians
parts.note: a shelf class in a library defined as being not made-up stories, so certainly not a novel

explanation.surface: A library shelving section that is anything but new.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' reads as 'new', suggesting an old, familiar category; it means a work of fiction, and this category is everything that is not.
explanation.definitionFit: Libraries split stock into fiction and factual books; the factual class is by definition never a novel.

clue.text: The Daleks were people's they say

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'The Daleks were people's they say': the only parse is Terry Nation's (the Daleks were Nation's) sounding like NATIONS (peoples); heard and spelt words share the same letters, apart from an apostrophe, so no homophone tree with distinct spellings exists
annotationWithheld.clue: The Daleks were people's they say

clue.text: "Elite" American fabricated by Banks?

definitions.meaning: the acronym for a White Anglo-Saxon Protestant, the old American establishment
Iain Banks wrote the novel The ... Factory, so this insect was made in his factory

explanation.surface: A so-called top-drawer American was a fake invented by bankers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' suggests money; it is the Scottish novelist Iain Banks, whose first novel was The Wasp Factory.
explanation.definitionFit: The acronym names the privileged white Protestant class, and the stinging insect is what Banks's factory produced.

clue.text: "He paused amd swallowed convulsively, like a taking a pill " (P. G. Wodehouse)

definitions.text: "He paused amd swallowed convulsively, like a taking a pill " (P. G. Wodehouse)

parts.words: "He paused amd swallowed convulsively, like a taking a pill " (P. G. Wodehouse)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation: the missing word is the small dog in Wodehouse's simile, between 'like a' and 'taking a pill'

explanation.surface: A Wodehouse character gulps like a lapdog forced to swallow medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue with its blank lost in print: the line reads 'like a ... taking a pill', and the gap is the toy dog breed from China.
explanation.definitionFit: Wodehouse compares the gulping man to a small Chinese toy dog being dosed with a pill.

clue.text: Steadfast paradigm for Keats

parts.note: Keats's sonnet opens by wishing he were as steadfast as a shining heavenly body, his model of constancy

explanation.surface: Keats's model of unwavering constancy.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats's last sonnet begins 'Bright star, would I were stedfast as thou art', so the star is his model of steadfastness and also the poem's title.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet takes a shining star in the night sky as his emblem of constancy, and the poem bears its name.

clue.text: "Every man has a lurking wish to —— considerable in his native place" (Samuel Johnson)

definitions.text: "Every man has a lurking wish to —— considerable in his native place" (Samuel Johnson)

parts.words: "Every man has a lurking wish to —— considerable in his native place" (Samuel Johnson)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Boswell's Johnson: the missing verb means to seem or look, before 'considerable'

explanation.surface: Johnson's remark that everyone secretly wants to look important at home.
explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: Johnson's line, recorded by Boswell, needs a verb meaning 'to seem' in the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson's line needs the verb meaning to seem or look, as in looking important in one's home town.

clue.text: The solitary horseman's French Calvinist

definitions.meaning: G. P. R. James, mocked for opening novels with a solitary horseman, wrote a novel of this title
a member of the Protestant Reformed church in sixteenth and seventeenth century France

explanation.surface: A lone rider turns out to be a French Protestant.
explanation.walkthrough: G. P. R. James was so often parodied for opening novels with 'a solitary horseman' that the phrase became his nickname; one of his novels has this title.
explanation.definitionFit: French Protestants of the Reformed church were known by this name; it is also the title of a James novel.

clue.text: Majestic end to La Gioconda's remark: "Don't make me laugh, — —"?

definitions.text: end to La Gioconda's remark: "Don't make me laugh, — —"?
definitions.meaning: the Mona Lisa, sitting for her portrait, might say 'I am sitting for a painter' in two words, I'M and POSING

explanation.surface: The Mona Lisa protests that she must not be made to smile, because she is sitting for her portrait.
explanation.walkthrough: La Gioconda is the Mona Lisa; her famous half-smile is explained by her saying she cannot laugh while she is sitting for the painter: 'I'm posing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something grand and stately in bearing makes a strong impression, which is what the adjective means.

clue.text: Austrian playwright provides me with two pupils

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: two asks for the piece that follows to be written twice

parts.note: L is a learner, a pupil, as on the L-plates of a learner driver

explanation.surface: A dramatist from Vienna supplies a writer with a couple of students.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two pupils' is two learners, each L, as on a British learner driver's L-plate. Max Mell was an Austrian dramatist.
explanation.definitionFit: Max Mell was an Austrian dramatist and poet of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Primal mess sorted out by old lady in Saint Mary Mead

definitions.text: old lady in Saint Mary Mead

indicators.note: sorted out suggests tidying a mess, so these letters are put into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An old lady tidies up a fundamental muddle in her village.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sorted out' reworks PRIMAL MESS. St Mary Mead is the village where Agatha Christie's elderly sleuth lives.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie's elderly amateur detective lives in the village of St Mary Mead.

clue.text: Nine Scotts, interchanged at random, seem much the same

indicators.note: letters interchanged at random are shuffled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Nine writers called Scott, swapped about, look much alike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interchanged at random' reworks NINE SCOTTS; 'seem' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unchanging or uniform throughout stays the same, which is what the adjective describes.

clue.text: Tennyson poem to identity published by Kathy Acker

definitions.meaning: Tennyson's long elegy for his friend Arthur Hallam

definitions.text: to identity published by Kathy Acker
definitions.meaning: Kathy Acker's 1990 novel is titled ... to Identity, so the first words complete that title

explanation.surface: A Tennyson elegy is dedicated to the self in a book from a punk novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Kathy Acker was an American experimental novelist whose book 'In Memoriam to Identity' borrows the Tennyson title.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson's elegy for Hallam carries this Latin title, which Acker reused for her novel about the self.

clue.text: Merchant's friend brings information on a sail come to grief

indicators.note: a sail that has come to grief is wrecked, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A friend of the merchant reports news about a sail that has been wrecked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'come to grief' reworks ON A SAIL. In The Merchant of Venice Salanio, Antonio's friend, brings the news of the wrecked ships, so 'brings information' fits the play.
explanation.definitionFit: Salanio is a friend of Antonio, the title character of The Merchant of Venice.

clue.text: Fewer means for Bennett's Hilda

parts.note: fewer means less
means are ways of doing something

explanation.surface: A writer's heroine has fewer methods at her disposal.
explanation.walkthrough: Hilda Lessways is the heroine of Arnold Bennett's novel of that name, in his Clayhanger series.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnold Bennett's heroine Hilda bears this surname, the title of his novel about her.

clue.text: Outstanding, like some of Strachey's subjects

definitions.meaning: Lytton Strachey's book of short lives was ... Victorians

explanation.surface: Remarkable, much like the figures Strachey wrote about.
explanation.walkthrough: Lytton Strachey's 'Eminent Victorians' (1918) mocked four Victorian worthies, the subjects referred to here.
explanation.definitionFit: Distinguished people stand out from the rest, and Strachey's four Victorian worthies were described so in his title.

clue.text: Fictional pig from Notting Hill?

definitions.meaning: the boar who seizes power in Orwell's Animal Farm
Chesterton's novel The ... of Notting Hill names its hero after the French emperor

explanation.surface: A pig in a novel comes from a smart London district.
explanation.walkthrough: Orwell's pig dictator and Chesterton's 'The Napoleon of Notting Hill' share the name; Notting Hill is a district of west London.
explanation.definitionFit: Orwell's tyrant pig and Chesterton's London leader both bear the French emperor's name.

clue.text: Biographer of Dickens finds a great weight removed in walled city

indicators.note: removed says the weight is taken away from the biographer's name

parts.note: G. K. Chesterton wrote a study of Charles Dickens
a ton is a large unit of weight

explanation.surface: A Dickens biographer drops a heavy load inside a city with walls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Biographer' suggests John Forster, Dickens's friend, but Chesterton also wrote a Dickens book; 'removed' takes TON from his name. Chester, in northwest England, keeps its Roman and medieval walls.
explanation.definitionFit: Chester in Cheshire is famous for its almost complete ring of Roman and medieval city walls.

clue.text: T. H. White's mistress can produce a song in her heart for ruralist writer

indicators.note: in her heart says one piece goes into the middle of the mistress's name

parts.note: T. H. White wrote the children's novel Mistress Masham's Repose
to produce a song is to sing

explanation.surface: A novelist's lady can sing from the heart for a countryside author.
explanation.walkthrough: T. H. White's children's book is 'Mistress Masham's Repose'. H. J. Massingham wrote about the English countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: H. J. Massingham was an English writer on the countryside and rural crafts.

clue.text: Indifferent, like Marryat's Jack and Muir's Tom?

definitions.text: like Marryat's Jack and Muir's Tom?
definitions.meaning: Frederick Marryat wrote ... Jack and Edwin Muir wrote ... Tom, so both titles share this adjective

explanation.surface: Mediocre, rather like a couple of literary characters called Jack and Tom.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Marryat's novel 'Poor Jack' and Edwin Muir's novel 'Poor Tom' share the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Indifferent work is of low quality, and the same adjective begins both the Marryat and the Muir titles.

clue.text: Spanish writer also gets say in another form

definitions.text: Spanish writer also gets say in another form

parts.words: Spanish writer also gets say in another form
parts.note: the philosopher's full name continues with y (Spanish for and, so also) and a surname that rearranges the letters of gets say

explanation.surface: A Spanish author gets to have his say in a different shape.
explanation.walkthrough: José Ortega y Gasset is the writer: 'also' is the Spanish y, and 'gets say in another form' rearranges to Y GASSET, the rest of his name, leaving the first surname as the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: José Ortega y Gasset was a Spanish philosopher and essayist, author of The Revolt of the Masses.

clue.text: Shakespeare should have tried a few of these, Ben Jonson seemed to think

definitions.text: Shakespeare should have tried a few of these, Ben Jonson seemed to think

parts.words: Shakespeare should have tried a few of these, Ben Jonson seemed to think
parts.note: Jonson, told Shakespeare never blotted a line, replied 'Would he had blotted a thousand', wishing for more revision

explanation.surface: Ben Jonson's view that Shakespeare ought to have revised his work more.
explanation.walkthrough: Jonson recorded that the players praised Shakespeare for never blotting out a line, and answered 'Would he had blotted a thousand' — he wanted more second drafts.
explanation.definitionFit: Second versions of a text, made by revising it, are what Jonson wished Shakespeare had produced.

clue.text: Next book by Durrell, with never a sequel

definitions.text: Next book by Durrell, with never a sequel

parts.words: Next book by Durrell, with never a sequel
parts.note: a Durrell novel whose Latin title means then or next; its sequel's Latin title means never

explanation.surface: Durrell's following book, which would never have a follow-up.
explanation.walkthrough: Lawrence Durrell's novel has a Latin title meaning 'then'; its sequel was 'Nunquam', Latin for 'never', so it does have a sequel — called Never.
explanation.definitionFit: Durrell's 1968 novel has a Latin title meaning then, and its sequel Nunquam means never.

clue.text: It's three feet long, but nowhere near a yard

definitions.text: It's three feet long, but nowhere near a yard

parts.words: It's three feet long, but nowhere near a yard
parts.note: a verse line of three metrical feet, which is short and has nothing to do with a yard of length

explanation.surface: Something measuring three feet that somehow falls well short of a yard.
explanation.walkthrough: Three feet make a yard, but here the feet are metrical units in a line of verse, so the line is short, not a yard.
explanation.definitionFit: A line of verse made of three metrical feet is named for its count of three measures.

clue.text: Scott family only at loggerheads

indicators.note: being at loggerheads means quarrelling and disordered, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A family in a Scott novel can do nothing but quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loggerheads' reworks ONLY AT, its own 'at' being part of the fodder. Paul Scott's Raj Quartet centres on the Layton family.
explanation.definitionFit: The Laytons are the army family at the centre of Paul Scott's Raj Quartet novels.

clue.text: A. P. Herbert felt that water was in several respects unsuitable for such purposes

definitions.text: A. P. Herbert felt that water was in several respects unsuitable for such purposes

parts.words: A. P. Herbert felt that water was in several respects unsuitable for such purposes
parts.note: Herbert's comic verdict that water was unfit for formal occasions and rites, as for toasting

explanation.surface: A. P. Herbert's view that water is the wrong drink for formal occasions.
explanation.walkthrough: A. P. Herbert, humorist and MP, wrote that water was unsuitable 'in several respects' for formal and ritual purposes.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal rites and occasions are what the adjective describes, purposes Herbert thought water unfit for.
